newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan says regrets China's Xinjiang riot deaths.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan says regrets China's Xinjiang riot deaths.

text.p: Taiwan said on Tuesday it regretted the deaths and injuries in separatist Moslem rioting in rival China's Xinjiang province and cautiously urged Beijing to respect ethnic minorities' customs and cultures.

"The Republic of China government (on Taiwan) feels sorry for the casualties that occurred during the riot in Xinjiang," said Chang King-yuh, chairman of Taiwan's top China policymaking body, the Mainland Affairs Council.

"We hope in dealing with minority races in the future China's communists can respect their culture, customs and language to maintain harmonious instead of turbulent relations with them," Chang said in a statement issued by state-funded Central News Agency.
China should "extensively review" relations with Xinjiang's Uighur minority and respect them, Chang said.

At least 10 people were killed, including one police officer, and some 100 wounded when 1,000 Moslem separatists rampaged through Yining on February 5 to protest against Beijing rule, Chinese sources and residents have said.

Residents said Chinese authorities have sealed off the town in the Yili Kazakh Autonomous Prefecture bordering Kazakhstan, closing its airport and railway station and imposing an after-dark curfew on the mainly Moslem town.
Exiled Uighur nationalists in Kazakhstan alleged on Tuesday that the riots were sparked by the execution of 30 Uighurs by Chinese authorities.

The riot was among the most violent for many years in restive Xinjiang, where Turkic-speaking Uighurs are in the majority and ethnic Han, China's main ethnic group, make up only 38 percent of the population.
Taiwan's statement was quite reserved, apparently a desire not to provoke Beijing over what one Mainland Affairs Council official called "a sensitive issue like this."

Beijing, which views Nationalist-ruled Taiwan as a rebel-held province, has regularly warned Taipei against any "splittist" moves of its own, saying it was ready to use force to prevent Taiwan from becoming an independent country.
